text: Fill in each blank with the correct protein, gene or peptide from the section on iron and copper disorders.
questions: In iron-deficiency anaemia, serum *ferritin:Which storage protein also serves as a serum marker of iron stores?* is low because body iron stores are genuinely depleted.
Total iron-binding capacity rises in iron deficiency because the liver makes more *transferrin:Which plasma transport protein carries iron?* to capture available iron.
In anaemia of chronic disease, interleukin-6 raises *hepcidin:Name the 25-amino-acid liver peptide that is the master regulator of iron.*, which degrades ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages.
Hereditary haemochromatosis is usually caused by the homozygous C282Y mutation of the *HFE:Which gene on chromosome 6 is most often mutated?* gene, leading to inappropriately low hepcidin.

Wilson disease results from defective *ATP7B:Which copper-transporting ATPase loads copper onto caeruloplasmin and excretes it into bile?*, causing copper to accumulate in the liver and brain with Kayser–Fleischer rings in the cornea.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hepcidin is the master switch separating iron-deficiency anaemia (low hepcidin, open ferroportin, low ferritin, high TIBC/transferrin) from anaemia of chronic disease (high hepcidin, trapped iron, normal/high ferritin). In hereditary haemochromatosis a mutant HFE gene keeps hepcidin inappropriately low despite overload, and in Wilson disease defective ATP7B causes copper toxicity.
